Euclidean geometry
in the asymptotic spectrum of tensors
OpenAI
November 24, 2026
Abstract
Over any field, we assign costs to tensors with indices placed in a real Hilbert space
so that a bit shared by two sites costs exactly their distance. On each finite set of two
or more sites, the costs are scaled logarithms of invariants that add under direct sums,
multiply under tensor products, and cannot increase under local linear maps. In every
such system, a bit shared among finitely many sites costs the mean width of their convex
hull, normalized to give a segment its length. For a triangle this is half its perimeter.
Companion papers use these costs to compare tensors with the networks that produce
them, yielding lower bounds for arithmetic circuits and an exponential bound on the size
of sunflower-free set families.

1

Introduction

Place the two indices of the tensor e0 ⊗ e0 + e1 ⊗ e1 at sites x and y. The indices carry
the same binary label. This tensor acts as a wire because contracting its first index with a
two-dimensional index of another tensor moves that index from x to y. Can an invariant of
placed tensors assign the wire itself its Euclidean length? We ask for one assignment that
works simultaneously for all pairs of sites and respects local linear maps on all tensors.
Strassen’s asymptotic spectrum supplies the algebraic rules for such an invariant [37]. A
spectral point on a fixed finite set of two or more sites assigns a nonnegative number F (T ) to
each tensor. Applying a linear map at each site is a restriction and cannot increase F . Tensor
products multiply its values, and direct sums add them. Here a direct sum places the two
tensors in separate blocks at every site. The normalization is F (0) = 0 and F (1) = 1. Taking
a logarithm turns multiplication into addition. We call a positive multiple of log2 F (T ) a
price, with log2 0 = −∞. Independent wires then have additive prices, and contracting wires
produces a tensor whose price is at most the sum of their prices.

Euclidean geometry in the asymptotic spectrum

Theorem 1.1 (Euclidean prices). Let k be any field and K any real Hilbert space. There is
a compatible assignment H(T ; x) to every tensor over k and every placement x = (x1 , . . . , xr )
of its indices in K with the following properties.
1. A binary wire between u and v costs ∥u − v∥. More generally, H(∆S (q)) = W (S) log2 q
for every nonempty finite S ⊂ K and every integer q ≥ 1.
2. For each finite set S ⊂ K of positive diameter there is a spectral point FS such that
H(T ; x) = W (S) log2 FS (T ) for every tensor placed in S. In evaluating FS , group the
indices at each site and adjoin a one-dimensional factor at each unused site. Compatibility
means that enlarging S leaves H(T ; x) unchanged.
3. For each nonzero T , the price depends on x only through the labeled distances ∥xi − xj ∥,
and H(T ; tx) = tH(T ; x) for t ≥ 0.

The shared-label formula is forced. Every compatible spectral system realizing the wire
distances on a whole Euclidean flat gives the same value for ∆S (q) (Theorem 5.3). For planar
sites whose convex hull is a polygon this value per bit is half the hull’s perimeter. Figure 1
illustrates why it matters which labels are shared. The formula also controls tensors carrying
a common label alongside other data. If a tensor already carries that label on S, appending
a copy at z increases its price by at most (W (S ∪ {z}) − W (S)) log2 q (Proposition 5.2). In
particular, a copy can be inserted anywhere on the segment joining two existing copies at
zero additional price. For arbitrary nonzero T , the chosen price is a seminorm on placements
modulo common translation. Applying a linear contraction to every site can only decrease
this price (Section 6).

1.1

Why a spectral point is needed

Across a cut of the sites, a tensor can be viewed as a matrix, and its matrix rank is a spectral
point. A binary wire has rank two across a cut separating its endpoints and rank one across
every other cut. Thus an average of log ranks measures how frequently the endpoints are
separated. Integrating over hyperplane cuts in Euclidean space recovers the length of a wire.
For each direction, the thresholds that split S form an interval whose length is the width of
the projection. Integrating these lengths recovers the mean width for the shared label.
The difficulty is extending these evaluations to a spectral point on all tensors at the
sites. For a small example, divide the four corners of a square by its vertical and horizontal
midlines. Let U be a horizontal wire and V a vertical wire. Their matrix ranks√across the
two cuts are (2, 1) and (1, 2), respectively. The geometric mean of the ranks is 2 for each

the metric obtained by averaging these two cuts is a rescaled Hamming square and violates
the four-point inequality (4.5) for spectral prices.
Direct sums matter for network constructions. If two tensors have the same output spaces,
their ordinary sum is a restriction of their direct sum. The price of a sum of m alternatives
on sites S is therefore at most their largest price plus W (S) log2 m. Compatibility lets us
use this bound even when the alternatives use different auxiliary sites. For a single graph
tensor, the tensor product of its edge wires [9], each edge of dimension q contributes its
length times log2 q. The wire formula gives the exact price of the graph tensor, and the sum
bound controls the price of alternative wirings.

1.2

Relation to earlier work

Strassen introduced the asymptotic spectrum to study transformations of large tensor
powers, motivated in particular by matrix multiplication [36, 37]. Comparison at all spectral
points characterizes asymptotic restriction. The difficult part in concrete applications is to
understand which evaluations can occur together. Strassen developed support functionals [38].
Christandl, Vrana and Zuiddam constructed quantum functionals yielding spectral points
over the complex field [10]. The relation between these constructions has since been clarified
by Hirai and by Sakabe, Doğan and Walter [14, 32]. For three-party tensors, Alman, Li and
Pratt study edge support functionals over arbitrary fields [2]. For higher-order tensors, Botero
and coauthors study obstructions to universality and the possibility of prescribing selected
evaluations [7]. Wigderson and Zuiddam survey the duality theory and the interpolation of
graph-tensor evaluations towards a single-mode flattening rank [39].
A triangle of independent wires represents matrix multiplication. Bounds for its asymptotic
rank constrain the three wire prices, and a shared-leg copying argument in [24] is related to
our incremental bound. Closure of price bounds under tensor degeneration follows from the
polynomial sublevel method of [11].
The other papers in this collection use different aspects of this framework. Shared labels
occur in the sunflower argument [29], and high-dimensional placements distinguish cuts of
arithmetic computations [26]. Spectral comparison and network compression enter the circuit
lower bounds [28]. Further applications concern Fourier transforms, integer multiplication on
tapes, and matrix multiplication [25, 27, 30].

1.3

Proof strategy

There are two questions. If a spectral space contains a Euclidean flat, which tensor prices
does its geometry force? And why must there be such flats in arbitrarily large dimensions? A
spectral flat of dimension d is a copy of Rd with compatible spectral prices whose binary wires
cost their Euclidean lengths. The existence statement that drives the proof is the following.
Theorem 1.2 (Existence of spectral flats). Over every field there is a spectral flat of every
positive finite dimension.
Part I derives the geometry from the algebra. The wire prices of any spectral point satisfy
the triangle inequality because two wires joined at a common end supply a wire between
their other ends. One can insert a new site at any prescribed position along an interval
(Theorem 3.1). Exterior algebra shows that when several indices move along their intervals

together, a tensor’s price is convex in their common parameter. A shifted crossing identity
then bounds the wire prices in a quadrilateral and gives nonpositive curvature in the sense
of Alexandrov (Theorem 4.3, following the terminology of [8]). Its two flattenings build on
crossing decompositions in [12, 17]. For the underlying Clifford algebra see [19].
On a Euclidean flat, interpolation implies that adding a site inside the convex hull of
the others leaves the price of their shared bit unchanged. A copying inequality and tensor
restrictions determine the price on segments and triangles. Approximating the support
function of a polytope by linear combinations of triangle support functions determines it
on every finite set (Section 5). Finally, given flats of unbounded dimension, concentration
on high-dimensional frames makes the prices of congruent placements agree in the limit.
This yields one system on the prescribed Hilbert space, including when its dimension is
uncountable (Section 6).
Assume there is a largest flat. The proof of Theorem 1.2 occupies Parts II and III.
Field transfer reduces its failure to a finite field with a largest flat dimension k ≥ 1. A
configuration approaching the corners of a Euclidean (k + 1)-cube could be filled in, rescaled,
and passed to a limit to give a larger flat. The bound on dimension thus excludes those
corners uniformly. The rest of the argument uses this geometric obstruction twice (Figure 2).

mean squared distance between all pairs of vertices by the mean squared distance along their

we must keep track of which tagged records have been routed to which vertices. A taggedpermutation gate tests that the addresses form a permutation and that their payloads
match. With these gates, the wire replacement gives an exact reduction in size per copy
(Proposition 14.1). Related methods of compressing wire assignments occur in algorithms for
satisfiability [23, Appendix D] and in crossing decompositions [12].
Implement the permutation gates. The second use of cube exclusion is local. Place k
pairs of distant wire endpoints along perpendicular axes at each tested location. If nearby
locations retain the prescribed prices for these wires, their motion can be read from the
changes in distances to the far ends. A transverse segment in the limit would produce the
excluded cube. These tests range over possible local spectral prices. A failed test allows a
local wire replacement, while successful tests identify a new link whose effect on subsequent
prices pays for its use. This gives an exact routing identity (Theorem 9.2). Terms that spend
too little on links between the layers have low enough price to discard. Routing the surviving
shorter lists recursively gives an approximation for 2h records with h-bit payloads using
O(2h h1+ε ) trivalent vertices for every fixed ε > 0 (Theorem 10.1).
The approximation has an algebraic meaning. Let I be the tensor product of wires
borrowed in the k coordinate directions. A network intended to compute f while returning
those wires produces a tensor X in the same spaces as f ⊗ I. Its error is the ordinary
difference X − f ⊗ I. After fixing the data indices, it suffices for the simulation that the
error have price less than H(I) by a specified margin in each prescribed flat placement of the
borrowed wires. The tagged-permutation approximation has this bound even with its data
indices exposed, as required for substitution. The margin pays for subsequent sums. Once
the margin exceeds the premium for adding two errors, a tensor cannot approximate two
distinct scalar multiples of I, since their difference has the full price H(I). Inserting these
approximate gates into the exact reduction and reusing borrowed wires along grid lines gives
Theorem 15.1. A bounded-degree computation of size V with sufficiently few external bits
then has an approximation of amortized size at most V /(log V )A for arbitrarily large fixed A.

Part I

The geometry of spectral prices

The calculus of prices

Every spectral point on a fixed set of parties gives a pseudometric on those parties. The
distance between two parties is the logarithm of the spectral point’s value on their binary
wire. We first show how the same invariant evaluates tensors on subsets of the parties and
controls the cost of moving their indices. All logarithms are to base two unless indicated
otherwise.

2.1

Spectral points and prices

Fix a field k and a finite set J of at least two parties. A tensor has one finite-dimensional
vector space at each party. We use bases throughout, and contraction is bilinear. Write
X ≤ Y when local linear maps, one at each party, take Y to X. Such a transformation
is a restriction. Two operations combine tensors on J. In a tensor product we group the
corresponding factors at each party. In a direct sum X ⊕ Y we take the direct sum of the
local spaces at every party, so the two summands occupy separate blocks. Up to mutual
restriction, these operations make the tensors a commutative semiring. Its integer r is the
